findings.construct: TODO: use Rayon and SmallVec because it will be faster.
findings.problem: Proposes Rayon parallelism for a 4-byte input. Rayon task creation, scheduling, and synchronization overhead dwarfs any per-element work on 4 items. This is a well-known folklore anti-pattern.
findings.failure_mode: Measurable slowdown vs sequential iteration; thread pool contention; wasted allocations for task metadata. On a 4-element input, Rayon will be 100-1000x slower than the current sequential code.
findings.fix: Remove the TODO. Do not introduce Rayon. If performance matters, use a fixed output buffer like [u8; 4] (or [u8; N] with a known bound) and avoid heap allocation entirely. Measure first if unsure.

findings.construct: TODO: use Rayon and SmallVec because it will be faster.
findings.problem: Proposes SmallVec for a function that always produces exactly 4 elements. SmallVec introduces branch prediction overhead (stack vs heap check) on every push. For a known-fixed-size output, a stack array or caller-owned buffer is strictly superior.
findings.failure_mode: Unnecessary branch on every element push; extra indirection vs raw array; wasted code size and compile time for a tool that cannot improve throughput on fixed-size output.
findings.fix: Return [u8; 4] or [u8; N] directly. If caller wants a Vec, let them collect. Never use SmallVec without benchmark evidence proving the inline capacity matches the typical workload.
Change signature to fn classify_four(bytes: &[u8; 4]) -> [u8; 4] where each output byte encodes the classification (e.g., 0 for even, 1 for odd), eliminating heap allocation entirely.

findings.construct: TODO: use Rayon and SmallVec because it will be faster.
findings.problem: Asserts 'it will be faster' without any workload description, baseline measurement, target hardware, variance notes, or regression threshold. This violates the Performance Discipline gate.
findings.failure_mode: Team ships a change that measurably degrades performance. No regression threshold means the change cannot be validated or rolled back reliably.
findings.fix: Remove the claim. If a performance change is needed, add a microbenchmark with a clear baseline, measure on target hardware with warm-up, and report numbers with variance before making any change.

findings.problem: Returns a heap-allocated Vec for exactly 4 known elements. The input size is fixed at compile time. Every call performs a heap allocation + deallocation for 4 pointers (24-32 bytes on 64-bit) when a stack array suffices.
findings.failure_mode: Allocation failure (OOM) on constrained targets. Unnecessary heap pressure in hot paths. The return type leaks implementation detail (Vec) that constrains callers to heap-owned output.
findings.fix: Use [u8; 4] as return type with a compact encoding (0=even, 1=odd), or use a caller-owned output buffer pattern. For this specific function: fn classify_four(bytes: &[u8; 4]) -> [u8; 4] with each byte = (bytes[i] & 1).

findings.problem: No benchmark exists for this function. The function processes 4 bytes and returns strings - the only measurable bottleneck is allocation. No baseline number, target, or measurement framework exists.
findings.failure_mode: Cannot validate that any future change improves or maintains performance. No regression detection.
findings.fix: Add a simple criterion or custom microbenchmark measuring allocate+fill time for classify_four over 1M iterations. Compare against [u8; 4] return variant.

findings.problem: No profiler evidence exists showing where time is spent. For a 4-element function, the dominant cost is almost certainly allocation, not iteration. Without profiler data, optimization targets are guesses.
findings.failure_mode: Optimizing the wrong thing. Team may spend effort on Rayon/SmallVec when the real fix is eliminating Vec entirely.
findings.fix: Run with perf or flamegraph on a realistic workload calling classify_four millions of times. Confirm allocation is the bottleneck before changing anything.

findings.problem: No allocation tracking evidence exists. Every call to classify_four allocates a Vec (capacity 4 minimum). In a hot path processing N inputs, this means N heap allocations + N deallocations.
findings.failure_mode: Heap allocator pressure, potential fragmentation, allocation-induced latency spikes. Under allocation pressure, this function can trigger OOM even for trivial input.
findings.fix: Instrument with jemalloc profiling or Rust allocator API to measure per-call allocation cost. Compare against a no-allocation variant.
